Most visitors eat in Dotonbori and stop there.
One stop from Osaka Station, the city eats on a 2.6 km covered street 👇

🍣 Harukoma is the oldest sushi shop there.
Plates from around ¥100.
Closed Tuesdays. Mid-afternoon is calmest.

🥔 Butchers fry croquettes at the counter.
That's the walking snack here.

🍻 After six, standing bars fill the lanes.
One drink, two plates, then the next bar.

Most visitors sleep in Namba.
Two neighbourhoods show where Osaka actually lives 👇

📍 Tenma
One stop from Osaka Station on the Loop Line.
A 2.6 km covered shopping street.
Tiny lantern-lit izakaya just north of JR Tenma.

📍 Tsuruhashi
Osaka's Korean neighbourhood.
Yakiniku the moment you leave the station.
Kintetsu trains to Nara stop here.

Four nights or a food trip? Try these two.

Do this 3-step check before you pay 👇

2️⃣ Expect a passport check.

🚃 Option 2: the Hakone-Yumoto desk
Drop it between 8:30 and 12:00.

¥1,500 regular, ¥2,500 large, one way.

🔒 Option 3: a locker at Odawara
L lockers in the Shinkansen passage, ¥800 a day.

A ¥3,000 ticket to one of Japan's biggest winter light shows, and ¥1,000 of it comes straight back as a voucher for dinner inside. That's Nabana no Sato near Nagoya this December 👇

🎯 Bet you can't guess which three nights cost almost double 👉 https://japanbystation.com/nabana-no-sato-illumination-2026?utm_source=facebook&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=fb_post

We went through the official 2026 price pages and bus timetables line by line.

✨ WHAT YOU SEE

Hana Kairo, a tunnel of light about 200 m long, then a 10-minute light-and-sound show, lights over water, and a tree that glows when the chapel bell rings. Autumn leaves are lit until late December too.

🎟️ WHAT IT COSTS

From 21 November to 22 December: ¥3,000 in advance, ¥3,200 at the gate. The voucher works for food and shopping, not the Island Fuji tower (¥800, cash only).

🎄 23–25 December is ¥5,500 with date-set advance tickets only.

🚌 GETTING THERE

From Nagoya: the direct bus from Meitetsu Bus Center, 4F, stop 22. About 30–35 minutes, ¥1,200 until 13 December (fares rise after that).

From Osaka: Kintetsu's set ticket from Namba covers trains, bus and entry, ¥7,930 in December.

🌸 The calm way: wait inside the heated Begonia Garden (included), eat early, and walk the tunnel 20–30 minutes after the lights come on.

Tokyo to Lake Kawaguchi with a big suitcase?
Bus or train? Here's how we'd choose 👇

🗺️ Full guide 👉 https://japanbystation.com/tokyo-to-kawaguchiko-big-suitcase-bus-or-train?utm_source=facebook&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=fb_post

🚌 Option A: the highway bus
💴 ¥2,000, and your case rides free in the hold.
🧳 One large suitcase per person.
You never lift it onto a rack.
📍 It leaves from Busta Shinjuku, 4th floor.
That's 2 minutes from JR Shinjuku's New South Gate.
🕕 Buses run from 6:45 to 22:25.
🚦 About 1 hour 45 minutes, but traffic can slow it.
No changes or refunds after departure.

🚆 Option B: the Fuji Excursion train
💴 ¥4,200, direct, with no traffic risk.
⏰ December weekdays from Shinjuku:
7:30, 8:30, 9:30 and 10:30.
🎫 Every seat is reserved.
Tickets go on sale a month ahead.
Weekends often sell out.

🔁 Option C: change at Otsuki
🚉 Take the Kaiji from Shinjuku, about an hour.
Then a Fujikyu local train (¥1,170).
🌙 Last weekday link: the 21:59 Kaiji.
It meets the 23:10 last train.

✅ Our take
Weekday, one case each? Take the bus.
Weekend, holiday or a booked tour?
Take the train. It can't get stuck in traffic.
Two big cases each? Train too.
The bus takes only one per person.

Half a day at Lake Kawaguchi by bike?
The lake is about 20 km around.
So pick one stretch of shore, plus lunch.
Your train home decides which 👇

😮 Full plan 👉 https://japanbystation.com/lake-kawaguchi-half-day-cycling?utm_source=facebook&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=fb_post

🚲 Short ride (train home at 14:58)
💴 Rent Q-BIKE, Fujikyu Railway's bike share.
It's ¥1,100 an hour in the app,
never more than ¥3,300 a day.
Two hours costs ¥2,200.
🌉 Ride to Kawaguchiko Ohashi Bridge
and Ubuyagasaki. Both are Fuji viewpoints,
about 1.6 km from the station.
🍽️ You're back by about 13:00 for lunch.

🚴 North shore (train home at 16:48)
🗻 Ride to Oishi Park, about 3.4 km away.
From there, you see Fuji's whole ridge.
🍲 Lunch: hoto noodles at Hoto Fudo's north store.
Open 11:00 to 19:00, every day.
🎫 Paper day pass at the station: ¥4,400.
Sold from 10:00. Bikes back by 17:00.

🚌 No bike at all
The Red Line bus reaches Oishi Park in 27 minutes.
It runs every 15 minutes.
A day pass is ¥1,500.
The 14:12 bus gets you back at 14:39.

✅ Our take
Early train home? Ride the short stretch.
On the 16:48? Ride the north shore.
Windy, wet or rushed? Take the bus,
then walk the lakeside path.

Going from Tokyo to Lake Kawaguchi?
Don't count on the direct train after lunch.
On December weekdays, the last regular one
leaves Shinjuku at 10:30 👇

🗺️ Route and map 👉 https://japanbystation.com/tokyo-to-kawaguchiko-big-suitcase-bus-or-train?utm_source=facebook&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=fb_post

❌ The mistake
You enjoy a slow morning in Tokyo.
Then you look for the direct train at noon.
But on weekdays there are only four:
7:30, 8:30, 9:30 and 10:30.
(Plus a seasonal 11:34 until 29 December.)
Every seat is reserved, on sale a month ahead.
At weekends, they're often gone.

✅ The fix
1️⃣ Leaving after 10:30?
Take the Kaiji limited express from Shinjuku.
It leaves at about half past each hour
and reaches Otsuki in about an hour.

2️⃣ At Otsuki, stay inside the station.
Walk through the transfer gate
to the Fujikyu platform.

3️⃣ Fujikyu trains leave 1 to 3 times an hour.
Example: the 12:30 Kaiji meets the 13:55 local.
Otsuki to Kawaguchiko is ¥1,170.
No seat ticket needed on the local.

4️⃣ Running late?
The last weekday link is the 21:59 Kaiji.
It meets the 23:10 last train.

🚌 Or take the bus from Busta Shinjuku.
It runs until 22:25 and costs ¥2,000 online.
One big suitcase per person rides free.

💡 Direct train showing no seats left?
There's a ticket without a seat number.
It's on the railway's own page, and in our guide.

Lake Kawaguchi: bike or bus?
A bike for ¥2,200, or a ¥1,500 bus pass?

🅰️ The bike
🚲 Q-BIKE is Fujikyu Railway's bike share.
In the app: ¥1,100 an hour, max ¥3,300 a day.
You need a credit card and a phone for SMS.
🎫 No card? Buy the ¥4,400 day pass
at the station's baggage storage, from 10:00.
Bring the bike back by 17:00.
🌬️ The best part: stop anywhere on the shore.
Worried about hills? Try an electric bike.

🦌 4 DEER RULES FROM NARA'S VISITOR BUREAU

1️⃣ Crackers only. Feed the deer the deer crackers sold in the park (¥200 a pack), never your own snacks.

2️⃣ One at a time. Hand them over one by one, not the whole stack at once.

3️⃣ Show empty hands. When you're out, open your arms and hands so they can see there's nothing left.

4️⃣ Bags and maps away. The bureau asks you to keep bags and maps out of reach of curious noses.

⚠️ AND TWO TIMES TO BE EXTRA CAREFUL

🍂 Autumn: the bureau warns that stags can turn aggressive, especially in this season.

🌱 Early summer: about 200 fawns are born each year at the Rokuen enclosure, and mothers are protective. Give them space.

They're wild animals that happen to be very used to people, and that's what makes walking among them so special. A little respect goes a long way.

Buying gift boxes in Japan to take home? Since 1 November 2026, tax-free shopping works differently: you pay the tax at the till and get it back at the airport, and eating one sweet can cost you the whole refund 👇

✅ THE NEW TAX-FREE CHECKLIST

1️⃣ Spend at least ¥5,000 before tax in the same store on the same day. Food and other items now count together.

2️⃣ Register the purchase at the store's tax-free counter. Some stores take a cut: Takashimaya deducts 23% of the tax amount as a fee.

3️⃣ Keep the boxes together and unopened. If anything from that purchase is missing or eaten when customs checks, nothing on it is refunded.

4️⃣ At the airport, scan your passport at customs before you check your bags, within 90 days of buying. Then the refund is paid out.

5️⃣ Eat the rest. Food you finish in Japan never counted anyway, so the taiyaki for the train is just a taiyaki.

The old sealed plastic bags are gone, which makes the food halls friendlier for gift shopping than before. The catch is simply: don't open the gift box.

✅ YATAI CHECKLIST

1️⃣ Go in twos or threes. Groups of 2 to 3 are ideal, and solo is fine. With about ten seats, five people rarely fit.

2️⃣ Bring cash. Most stalls are cash only; only about 10% take credit cards.

3️⃣ Leave the suitcase. Stalls are tiny, so drop bags at the hotel or a locker first.

4️⃣ Ask, then order. Say "two people, OK?", check the prices, and order at least one drink and one dish each. Pay when you leave.

5️⃣ Check the weather. There are no fixed holidays, and many stalls stay closed in rain or wind.

🍢 What to order: tonkotsu ramen, yakitori and oden are standard everywhere. Yaki-ramen and mentaiko tamagoyaki are the local favourites, and no stall serves raw food.

The best part isn't on the menu: you sit elbow to elbow with whoever's there, and the cook is part of the conversation.

In Fukuoka, the udon is soft on purpose, the mackerel is eaten raw, and the hotpot ends with a pile of noodles. Most visitors only eat the ramen. Here's how locals eat the rest 👇

🍜 Hungry yet? The spots, hours and prices 👉 https://japanbystation.com/fukuoka-food-beyond-tonkotsu-ramen?utm_source=facebook&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=fb_post

🍥 HAKATA UDON

Soft and tender, in a clear broth of flying fish, anchovy, bonito and kelp, with goboten (burdock tempura) on top. At Makino Udon, by Hakata Station, each bowl comes with a little kettle of extra broth, because the noodles keep drinking it up.

🐟 GOMA SABA

Raw mackerel in sesame-soy. Mackerel spoils fast, so most of Japan doesn't eat it raw. Fukuoka's fresh catch makes it possible. Hakata Gomasaba-ya near Akasaka serves it at lunch for ¥1,000.

🍲 MOTSUNABE

A beef offal hotpot. The local move is the finish: champon noodles go into the broth at the end. Pace yourself.

🐔 MIZUTAKI

A chicken hotpot where you drink a cup of the plain broth before anything goes in.

🍜 AND THE RAMEN, ORDERED PROPERLY

Say your firmness (barikata = a little firm), and when the noodles are gone, order kaedama, a refill for your soup. Fukuoka's tourism site suggests one step softer the second time, because the soup has cooled.
